The scalp biopsy shows dense dermal fibrosis with thick, whorled/onion‑skin collagen bundles, marked loss/distortion of hair follicles, perifollicular fibroplasia and ectatic capillaries — histology that is characteristic of a fibrous cephalic plaque (a TSC‑specific lesion). The facial biopsy shows angiofibroma, a major diagnostic cutaneous feature of TSC. Although there is no reported neurologic involvement or family history, TSC has highly variable expressivity and cutaneous signs often present in childhood. Other entities that can produce firm alopecic plaques with increased dermal collagen or facial papules are considered but are less consistent with the combination of findings and histology.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Tuberous sclerosis complex (cutaneous manifestations: fibrous cephalic plaque of the scalp + facial angiofibromas + ash‑leaf macules/shagreen‑type lesion) — most likely
2. Isolated connective tissue nevus (collagenoma / sporadic collagenoma) — can produce a firm, scarlike collagenous plaque with alopecia but does not explain coexisting angiofibromas and ash‑leaf macules
3. Keloid / hypertrophic scar (keloidal collagenoma) — histology can show dense whorled collagen bundles and onion‑skin fibroplasia, but clinical history of prior trauma/surgery and distribution make this less likely
4. Nevus sebaceus (organoid nevus) of the scalp — congenital alopecic plaque on the scalp that can develop papules, but histology and presence of facial angiofibromas/ash‑leaf macules argue against this as the unifying diagnosis
5. Birt‑Hogg‑Dubé syndrome (fibrofolliculomas / trichodiscomas) — produces multiple facial dome‑shaped papules and collagenous skin findings, but histology (fibrofolliculoma) and associated systemic features differ from the angiofibromas and fibrous cephalic plaque seen here

A man in his 20s presented with a 6-year history of multiple growing papules superimposed on an asymptomatic firm plaque on the occipital scalp. The lesions were never ulcerated or inflamed, but hemorrhage occurred occasionally after rubbing. At 3 years of age, scarlike macules appeared on the occipital scalp and coalesced to form a larger plaque with sparse hair. Simultaneously, multiple brown-red, dome-shaped papules developed on the nose and gradually evolved to involve the cheeks. Rubbery plaques also developed on the sacrococcygeal area, along with hypopigmented patches on the right buttock. The patient has no systemic symptoms or mental impairment and denied a family history of genetic disease.
